_comment: Everything deployment-specific for sched.py. The script hardcodes NOTHING about a
machine, an owner or a timezone - point SCHED_CONFIG at a copy of this file and you
have an independent scheduler.
Three keys are REQUIRED and fatal when absent, because silently defaulting any of
them produces a scheduler that looks like it is working:
owner.claude_config_dir - a wrong value means the daemon refuses to run, or worse,
the WRONG agent runs it and does another fleet's work.
db.path                 - a wrong value means an empty database, which is
indistinguishable from 'nothing is due today'.
defaults.tz             - a daily 09:00 job that quietly runs at 09:00 UTC when the
deployment is in Tokyo is off by nine hours and nobody gets
an error about it.
Everything else has a default. Env vars still outrank this file: SCHED_CONFIG,
SCHED_DB, SCHED_TICK_SECS, SCHED_EVAL_TIMEOUT_SECS.
JSON has no comments, so this file documents itself with _comment keys. The loader
strips every leading-underscore key, so they can never be read as data.
The ONLY CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR allowed to run the daemon. Every other agent that arms
it exits 0 with a SCHED-GUARD line, so a shared 'arm at session start' rule is safe
to give the whole fleet.
⚠️ LIVE DURABLE STATE - every schedule the fleet has ever been given lives in this
one file. It is deliberately NOT under XDG_CACHE_HOME (a cache is a place things
get deleted from) and NOT under the agent's CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR (the harness owns that
directory and sweeps it); the agent home's state/ directory is the place. The
single-instance lock sits beside the DB, so unlike a chat watcher there is no
environment variable that can silently fork the state.
⚠️ Deleting this file does NOT stop the schedules. Every task re-arms from an empty
state on its next evaluation and fires nothing until its next due time - so a daily
job quietly skips a day and reports nothing. Use `sched.py cancel`, never `rm`.
path: an ABSOLUTE path; a leading ~ is expanded.
⚠️ SET THIS BEFORE USE. IANA name; per-task tz overrides it. Defaulted to UTC here,
which is almost certainly wrong for you - a wall-clock schedule is a LOCAL concept.
Per-task tz overrides it; this is what `add` uses when nobody says.
Wall-clock schedules ('daily at 09:00') are a LOCAL concept - storing them in UTC
drifts by an hour twice a year and the symptom is a report arriving at the wrong
time, not an error.
tick_secs 1.0 is affordable: evaluation costs ~35us per task per tick, so 50 tasks
is under 0.2% of a core. The binding constraint is EMIT volume, not CPU - see emit.
resync_lag_secs: after a suspend or a stalled disk the loop resyncs its pacing
instead of bursting through the missed ticks. Bursting would call every predicate
N times with nearly the same `now`, which is wasted work at best and a flood at
worst. Predicates are edge-triggered, so one evaluation at the new time is exact.
timeout_secs is enforced with signal.setitimer, which takes floats - signal.alarm
would round up to a whole second, making the smallest enforceable bound a full tick.
max_errors: consecutive predicate failures before the task is marked failed. A bad
RETURN SHAPE fails on the first strike instead, because it is deterministic and
retrying it just produces three identical log lines.
max_due_slots bounds the coalescing helper so a task resumed after a year of
downtime folds into one fire instead of walking 8760 hours inside the timeout.
⚠️ min_interval_secs is a FLOOR THE DAEMON ENFORCES regardless of what a predicate
returns. A snippet stuck at fire=True would otherwise inject 3600 wake-up lines an
hour into the agent's session and make it unusable. Trusting every future snippet's
arithmetic not to do that is not a plan.
max_line_chars is larger than the Slack watcher's 500 because here the instruction
IS the payload, not a preview. Nothing structural is ever truncated - an over-long
payload degrades into a pointer to `sched.py show <id>`.
reason_chars caps the task's REASON, which is emitted BEFORE the instruction. The
line budget cuts from the end, so reason-first is what stops a long instruction
silently swallowing the reason on the one wake-up where the agent most needs it;
this cap is what stops the reason doing the same to the instruction in return.
⚠️ Setting it to 0 does NOT turn the reason off gracefully - it drops below the
floor in format_emit, and the reason segment is omitted whole rather than
rendered as an empty stub. That is deliberate: a `why:` carrying no why spends
the instruction's budget to say nothing.
requester_chars caps the `by=` field, which is PREFIX and therefore comes out of
the payload's budget. It also holds human text now, so it is quoted on the line:
the prefix is a space-separated field list and a display name contains spaces.
Turns the id a request arrives with into the name a human recognises, so a task
row and a wake-up line say `by=Ada` and not `by=UEXAMPLE99`. All three keys are
optional; the two directory keys default to no directory.
directory_file: a JSON file - typically the chat integration's own config, so
there is ONE roster on the machine and not a second copy here
that drifts. Read on demand, never at import: an install with no
roster, or one whose copy is briefly unreadable, must still run.
An ABSOLUTE path; a leading ~ is expanded.
directory_key:  the dotted path to the id-to-name object inside that file.
id_pattern:     what an unresolved id LOOKS like. A `--requester` matching this
that the directory cannot resolve is REFUSED outright. null (the
default) derives it: the alternation of every WORKING chat
transport's user-id shape (`ids.user` in its transport.json), so
it follows the transports this fleet runs. Set a regex only to
narrow or widen that on purpose.
⚠️ That refusal is the point, and softening it to a warning defeats the whole
block. Storing the id satisfies every constraint and every test; the failure
surfaces months later as a task whose only record of who wanted it is a string
nobody can identify.
`add` dry-runs every predicate before it reaches the database and REFUSES two
outcomes without --force: zero fires in the horizon (a dead schedule, which is
silent for weeks) and more than fires_per_day_warn per day (a runaway, which is
loud and immediate). These are the two mistakes an authored snippet actually makes.
A missing --reason is refused too, and that one --force does NOT override: a
schedule whose purpose was never written down is the mistake with the longest fuse.
auto_archive_days: terminal tasks older than this flip to 'archived' and leave the
default list view. runs_per_task trims run history at insert, so growth is bounded
with no cron. Nothing here ever DELETES - only `purge --yes` does, and never
automatically.
